column4: The verse sets people who call their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face, against one who wants the adornment of worldly life and follows desire; this closely meets the section’s turn from broad worldly longing to the Lord.
The parable begins with two men, one given two gardens; it is another concrete garden scene that frames the section’s lost-garden owners and their changed appeal to God.
The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and followers, supplying the worldly confidence that contrasts with the section’s later appeal to the Lord after loss.

The boastful owner assumes that, if returned to his Lord, he will receive an even better return; this makes his expectation of worldly gain a false counterpart to the section’s humble hope in the Lord.
The other man says Allah is his Lord and he associates no one with Him, giving a direct contrasting stance within the same garden story.
The believing companion tells the owner to acknowledge Allah’s will and power when entering the garden, making the source of worldly provision explicit.
The companion says his Lord may give him a better garden and send a calamity upon the other; this anticipates the section’s garden owners hoping their Lord will replace what they lost.
The companion warns that the garden’s water could sink beyond recovery, naming the concrete limit on the owner’s apparent security.
After his garden is destroyed, the owner regrets that he associated anyone with his Lord; it is a close parallel to the section’s owners turning toward their Lord after losing a garden.
No faction can help the ruined owner against Allah, adding the collapse of worldly support to the garden-loss scene.
The passage concludes that true protection belongs to Allah and that He gives the best reward and outcome, identifying the Lord as the lasting source of support.
The command فَفِرُّوا إِلَى ٱللَّهِ directly names movement toward God, paralleling the section’s direction إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ.
The next verse forbids setting another deity alongside Allah, making the exclusivity of fleeing toward Him explicit.
The Prophet is told to become upright toward God and seek His forgiveness; it joins an upright stance with a directed return to Him.
The command to set one’s face toward worship and call on God sincerely gives a concrete posture and act for the section’s exclusive Godward desire.
The Prophet says his prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are for Allah, Lord of the worlds; this gives the section’s direction toward the Lord a whole-life form.
The next verse adds that Allah has no partner and that this was commanded, sharpening the exclusivity stated in 6:162.
The verse says whoever hopes to meet his Lord should do righteous work and associate no one in worship with Him, joining effort, hope, and exclusive orientation.
People leave their beds to call their Lord in fear and hope and spend from what He provided; this brings rising, exertion, directed prayer, and divine provision into one image.
The next verse says no soul knows what comfort has been hidden for these workers as recompense for their deeds, connecting their effort to an abundant gift from God.
Those invoked besides God themselves seek access to their Lord, hope for His mercy, and fear His punishment; this explicitly describes desire directed toward the Lord with hope and fear.
The verse commands calling on the Lord in fear and hope, a repeated formulation of the posture described in 21:90.

The Prophet is told not to fix his eyes on worldly adornments given to others because his Lord’s provision is better and more lasting; this directly counters the section’s secondary image of broad desire for the world.
The next command is to keep the family at prayer and be patient in it, since Allah provides; it joins sustained effort in worship to provision from the Lord.
The Prophet is told to perform extra prayer at night in hope that his Lord will raise him to a praised station, joining night effort to hope in the Lord’s gift.
The righteous are described as sleeping little at night; this is another concrete night-devotion scene beside the section’s command to rise at night.
The same people seek forgiveness before dawn, completing the night-to-day devotion scene introduced in 51:17.
After help and victory arrive, the Prophet is told to glorify his Lord with praise and seek forgiveness; a completed mission turns directly into Godward action.

The verse says some people’s effort is lost in worldly life although they think they are doing good, a direct counterpart to the section’s warning that exertion can be wasted if it lacks the right direction.

The following verse says their deeds carry no weight on the Day of Resurrection because they rejected their Lord’s signs and meeting Him, supplying the reason and outcome for the lost effort in 18:104.
God promises not to waste any worker’s work, then names migration, expulsion, suffering, and struggle for His cause; it is the positive counterpart to labor that comes to nothing.
Those who recite the Book, establish prayer, and spend from God’s provision hope for a trade that will never fail, joining effort and worship to a lasting return.
The next verse says God will pay their wages in full and increase them from His bounty, specifying the gift behind their hoped-for return.
During the pilgrimage, people are to witness benefits and mention Allah’s name over the livestock He provided; it joins completed ritual, remembrance, and provision from God.
The next verse tells pilgrims to complete their rites, fulfill their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House, extending the Hajj scene around the remembrance named in 22:28.
For every community a rite is appointed so they mention Allah’s name over the livestock He provided; the verse connects worship to gifts from the one God.
The sacrificial camels are made among God’s signs, and His name is mentioned over them; it gives a concrete form to sacrifice directed to the Lord.
The next verse says neither meat nor blood reaches Allah, but God-consciousness does; it clarifies that sacrifice’s Godward intention, not its material object, is what matters.
The verse contrasts one who wants the harvest of the Hereafter, whose yield God increases, with one who wants the harvest of this world; it joins work and the direction of desire.
Those who want worldly life and its adornment are paid for their deeds in this life but receive no share beyond it, a direct boundary on worldly-directed labor.
The next verse states their Hereafter outcome and that their deeds have come to nothing, completing the warning in 11:15.
Wealth and children are called adornment of worldly life, while lasting good deeds are better with the Lord as reward and hope; this gives a precise world-versus-enduring-work boundary.
After describing a sealed drink for the righteous, the verse says to let those who compete compete for it, redirecting aspiration toward an abundant divine gift.
The tranquil soul is called to return to its Lord, satisfied and accepted; this adds a personal return and satisfaction to the section’s claim that the destination is the Lord.
The address offers a trade that saves from painful punishment, setting up the section’s image of effort yielding a gift from God.
That trade is specified as faith and striving in Allah’s cause with wealth and lives, making exertion explicitly God-directed.
The following verse names forgiveness and Gardens as the return for that striving, completing the passage’s divine reward.
Allah is described as purchasing believers’ lives and property in exchange for the Garden; this concretely joins the Lord’s ownership, human effort, and abundant reward.
Before the address in 55:31, this verse says all in the heavens and earth ask God and He is each day in an affair, adding the ongoing divine activity behind the section’s use of farag for God.
The verse commands people to turn toward their Lord and submit to Him, directly paralleling the section’s direction إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ.
